17122-twenty-four-short-sermons-on-the-d:
John Bovee Dods, pastor of the First Universalist Society in Taunton, Massachusetts, preached these twenty-four short sermons in 1832. They defend universal salvation: the hope that all souls at last find grace. The first sermon starts from Psalm 34, on desiring life and loving many days, and links duty, health, happiness, and long life in one cup.

Dods writes in plain pulpit prose, with scripture texts, moral counsel, and a warm, hopeful tone. His sermons suit readers curious about Universalist thought in early America. The set gives a clear, earnest statement of a faith that stressed God's wide mercy over endless punishment.
21707-ungava:
Fur traders push into the wild country around Hudson's Bay in this early novel by R. M. Ballantyne. In his introduction, Ballantyne says most of the main events really happened to the first settlers of Ungava. He reshaped real people and real dangers into a story, with their leader's own records as his base.

The tale opens in deep forest, with a rifle shot, hard counsel, and a narrow escape on an ice floe. Ballantyne had worked for the Hudson's Bay Company as a young man, so the cold, the travel, and the trade feel lived-in. It stands as one of the books that made his name with young readers.
21918-hindu-law-and-judicature-from-the-:
Ancient Hindu law reaches English readers in this 1859 translation of the law chapters of the Dharma-Shastra of Yajnavalkya. Edward Röer, a scholar of Sanskrit, worked with W. A. Montriou, a barrister, to join exact rendering with legal sense. The preface says a connected, explained translation was a practical want, and a long list of subscribers in India agreed. The great commentary, the Mitakshara, supplies the staple of their notes.

The rules cover courts, evidence, debts, inheritance, and the duties of kings in judgment. Yajnavalkya stands with Manu among the lawgivers of classical India. For British judges and Indian lawyers of 1859, this was a working tool. For readers now, it opens the legal mind of an old civilization in its own terms.
25355-rollo-in-geneva:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo in Geneva, published in New York in 1867, follows twelve-year-old Rollo with his parents, his younger brother Thanny, his cousin Jane, and his uncle Mr. George. It belongs to Rollo's Tour in Europe, a series meant to teach geography through story.

The party plans a ride to Geneva, explores the town and hotel, and rides into the environs to see the junction of the Arve and the Rhone. They watch Mont Blanc go out at sunset, sail the lake to Villeneuve, and visit the Castle of Chillon. A walk to Aigle, jewelry shopping, and a fortunate accident round out the tour.
27552-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Charles Burke's Rip van Winkle appears in this volume of Representative Plays by American Dramatists, covering 1856 to 1911. The introduction tells the history of the play's evolution, in which many hands were concerned.

Its growth in scenic effect and dialogue was a stage growth, not one prompted by literary fervour. No dramatization, the writer says, approached Washington Irving's original in art or vividness of scene. Yet actors vied with Irving in characterization, and Jefferson's classic portrayal stands above every other memory, while Burke and Herne earn recall for their Dutch lifelikeness. The piece shows how an actor's personality made dry bones live.
27556-across-the-equator-a-holiday-trip-:
Thos. H. Reid published this holiday trip in Java with Kelly and Walsh in Singapore, Shanghai, Hong Kong, and Yokohama in 1908. A temple at Parambanan fronts the volume, and Reid visited Java at the end of September 1907 for a brief vacation.

The book grew from articles in the Straits Times, reprinted after many requests, then revised and amplified. Reid makes no pretense of an exhaustive guidebook. Instead, he arranges chapters so a visitor can follow a route west to east in a fortnight or three weeks. Photographs of Tosari and the volcanic east enrich the journey.
4073-ex-voto-an-account-of-the-sacro-mon:
An account of the Sacro Monte, or New Jerusalem, at Varallo describes a hillside shrine where painting and sculpture grew endemic in North Italy. Varallo, the most western city of that art, stands apart from Turin, Novara, and Vercelli, which held no like tradition.

A chapter on Bernardino Caimi and Fassola traces the shrine's makers and their chapels, where life-size figures stage the life of Christ. The book mixes travel, art history, and devotion, with close notes on artists east of Milan. Readers who love Italian art and pilgrimage places will find a rich, detailed guide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altamura-and-: Altamura and Acquaviva form an exempt archipresbyterate in Bari province, southern Italy. Altamura was made exempt from a bishop's rule by Innocent IV in 1248 and again by Innocent VIII. Acquaviva, a country town, was made exempt too by Pius IX and united with it in August 1848. Altamura has 4 parishes and 19,333 Catholics; Acquaviva has one parish and 8,527 Catholics; the clergy number 80.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-canov:
Possagno-born Antonio Canova, who lived from 1757 to 1822, is presented here as the leading Italian sculptor of modern times. Taught first by his grandfather, a skilled stone cutter, he could model clay and carve small marble shrines before he was ten. A Venetian senator placed him with the sculptor Torretto, and monks later lent him a vacant cell for a studio. At sixteen he modelled Eurydice, followed three years later by Orpheus.

Daedalus and Icarus showed his gift for dramatic movement, and a move to Rome in 1780 put him face to face with ancient sculpture, which gave his talent fresh force. Theseus and the Minotaur, made in 1782, counts among his finest works. The article follows a boy carver from a small town workshop to the centre of European art, tracing how study of the antique shaped his calm, classical style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ava:
Ava was a German poet, the first woman known to write in German. She was probably the recluse of that name who died near Melk in Austria in 1127. Almost nothing is known of her life or person. She tells us she was the mother of two sons. Those sons helped her gather material for her poems.

Her poems are verse versions of New Testament stories. They cover the Life of Jesus, the Antichrist, the Holy Ghost's gifts, the Last Judgment, and John the Baptist. Two manuscripts preserve them, one at Verona and one at Gorlitz, and John the Baptist appears only in the second. Her authorship of that poem and of the Life of Jesus has been questioned, but hardly on strong grounds. The poems are naive and deeply religious, though mostly without poetic merit, and their technique is often crude, with assonance standing in for rhyme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bova:
Bova, a Calabrian diocese suffragan to Reggio, was peopled about 1477 by Albanian refugees fleeing the Turks after Scanderbeg's death. These Albanians kept the Greek rite until Gregory XIII's reign. An older claim makes Luminosus, present at the Lateran Council of 649, its first bishop, but he was in truth Bishop of Bologna, and Bova town arose much later.

Its most distinguished bishop, Achille Brancia, sat at Trent in 1549. The diocese holds about 20,000 souls in 14 parishes, with 34 churches and chapels, 34 secular priests, and 25 seminarians. Its story shows a refugee community that kept its Greek rite for a century before it passed from use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudius-acqu:
Claudius Acquaviva, fifth General of the Society of Jesus, was born in October 1543 and died on 31 January 1615. Prince Giovanni Antonio Acquaviva, Duke of Atri, was his father, he stood high in favour at the papal court at twenty-five. Then he renounced worldly prospects and entered the Society. After serving as Provincial of Naples and Rome, he won election as General on 19 February 1581. 

His generalship faced persecution in England, Huguenot troubles in France, crushing of Christianity in Japan, and expulsion from Venice. A schism loomed within the Society, and pope, Inquisition, and Philip the Second were hostile. Yet his prudence, skill, courage, and success make him the Society's greatest administrator after Saint Ignatius, in the article's judgment. His hardest trial was the Spanish schism organised by Vasquez. King and pope were won over, and demands for Spanish quasi-independence were met at last through the English Jesuit Robert Parsons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cordova:
The entry covers the Diocese of Cordova, Cordubensis in America, in the Argentine Republic, suffragan of Buenos Aires. Created in 1570, the see lay vacant from 1819 to 1830, and again from 1841 to 1858. It counts 46 parishes and 49 churches and chapels. Its vast extent, including the two states of Cordova and Rioja, which in 1895 held about 570,000 souls, gives it two auxiliary bishops.

The episcopal city itself counts 53,000 people. One of the two national universities, the second oldest in the New World, founded 1573, sits there, along with a national observatory and also a meteorological bureau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-andrada:
Diego Andrada de Payva was a Portuguese theologian born at Coimbra in 1528. He taught theology at his own university before King Sebastian sent him to the Council of Trent in 1561. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry praises the defense of papal authority he wrote there. That work earned him the special thanks of the pope.

His Ten Books of Orthodox Explanations answered the Lutheran Chemnitz point by point. His Defense of the Tridentine Faith replied to Chemnitz in turn, reaching as far as the teaching on the Immaculate Conception. The entry also notes his three volumes of Portuguese sermons. He died at Lisbon in 1575 with his great defense still unfinished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-viva:
Domenico Viva was a Jesuit writer born at Lecce on 19 October 1648. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1663 and taught the humanities and Greek, then philosophy, moral theology, and scholastic theology for years. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces him to the Naples College rectorship in 1711, and later to head of the Naples province.

His works include a handbook on the jubilee and indulgences, a school course of theology, and short moral treatises for students. His most famous work, the Theological Balance of condemned theses from 1708, won praise from Saint Alphonsus Liguori and others. He died on 5 July 1726, a teacher whose books stayed in use long after him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eulogius-of-c:
Eulogius of Cordova was a ninth-century Spanish martyr and writer who lived under the Muslim rulers of Cordova. He was born before 819 to a noble family long settled in the city. He studied in the monastery of Saint Zoilus, formed a close friendship with the scholar Alvarus, and was ordained a priest by Bishop Recared. By 848 he stood high among the Christians of Catalonia and Navarre, in a land where Christians kept their churches but paid heavy taxes.

His writings are the chief record of Spanish Christianity from 848 to 859. Above all they tell of the martyrs who died in the persecution under the caliphs. Toledo chose him archbishop shortly before his beheading on 11 March 859. He was buried in the cathedral of Oviedo. Readers come here for a vivid life, a portrait drawn by his friend, and a firsthand account of a church living under foreign rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gian-paolo-ol:
Gian Paolo Oliva was a Jesuit preacher and superior born at Genoa in 1600, who died at Rome in 1681. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1616 and became Apostolic Preacher of the Palace under four popes, from Innocent X to Clement X. In 1661, during a troubled generalate, the congregation elected him vicar-general with right of succession. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents him as a peacemaker among religious orders.

His chief aim was to end friction between his order and others, toward whom he showed reverence and yielding. He spread the missions beyond Europe, above all in Japan, and preached forty-odd Lenten sermons. His six-volume commentary on chosen passages of Scripture shows his learning and piety. Mindful of how Cardinal Palavicino's letters had been misused, he printed a thousand of his own so others could not twist them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermopolis-pa:
Hermopolis Parva was a titular see of Egypt, suffragan to Alexandria, whose ancient name means town of Horus. The Copts called it Tuininhor and the Arabs Damanhur, a town on the canal joining Lake Mareotis to the Nile's Canopic branch. No history of its own belongs to it, and no ruins, yet its bishops' list reaches back into the fourth century.

Among those bishops were Dracontius, exiled for the faith under Constantius around 354, St. Isidore his successor, and Dioscorus, eldest of the four Tall Brethren of Nitria. Near Damanhur, Bonaparte narrowly escaped capture by Mamelukes on 10 July 1798. Modern Damanhur, forty miles from Alexandria, is chief town of Behera province and famed for silk, linen, and cotton goods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hosius-of-cor:
Hosius of Cordova led the West's defence of orthodoxy in the early struggle against Arianism, born about 256 and dead about 358. In early life he confessed the faith under persecution, then took Cordova's bishopric in southern Spain about 295. His name appears among nineteen bishops at the provincial Council of Elvira around 300.

Hosius stood in close personal relations with Emperor Constantine between 313 and 324 and served as his chief adviser on the Donatists. When Arian troubles began, Constantine charged him with delivering a letter urging Arius and Alexander to reconcile. At Nicaea, Hosius presided with the Roman priests Vitus and Vincent, though whether he acted in the pope's name remains much discussed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joao-mendes-d:
João Mendes de Silva, better known as Amadeus of Portugal, was born in 1420 and died at Milan in 1482. He began religious life with the Hieronymites at Guadalupe for about ten years, then joined the Franciscans in Italy, living chiefly at Milan, where virtue and miracles drew notice.

Under Milan's archbishop Amadeus founded Our Lady of Peace in 1469, centre of a Franciscan reform backed by Minister-General Rovere, later Sixtus IV. His houses, called Amadeans, reached twenty-eight in Italy, with Saint Peter in Montorio at Rome chief among them, and Innocent VIII gave them a Spanish house in 1493. His treatise on revelations and prophecies remains unpublished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-cordo:
Juan de Córdova was a Spanish Dominican who gave the Zapotec people a dictionary and grammar. Born at Cordova in 1503, he served as a soldier in Flanders, sailed with Coronado to New Mexico in 1540 to 1542, and joined the Dominicans at Mexico in 1543. Sent to Oaxaca in 1548, he learned Zapotec and served its Indians.

Named provincial in 1568, Córdova ruled with military rigor until complaints led to his suspension in 1570. Accepting deposition with the words Benedictus Deus, he retired to Tlacochauaya for twenty-five years of study. His Zapotec vocabulary of 1571 and his Zapotec art of 1578 also record Zapotec rites, superstitions, and time reckoning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-la-cu:
Juan de la Cueva was a Sevillian poet and dramatist who helped break Spanish drama from classical rules. Born of a noble family at Seville in 1550, he visited the West Indies and lived in Portugal, but his fame rests on plays staged from 1579 onward. Few survive, yet most were historical in subject.

Cueva ignored Greek and Latin models, slighted the classical unities, cut the acts from five to four, and brought new verse forms to the stage. His plays treat Bernardo del Carpio, the Seven Princes of Lara, Ajax, and the Sack of Rome, while El Infamador foreshadows Tirso's Don Juan. Faults remain: all ranks speak loftily, and tangles end in sudden murder or marvel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lausanne-and-:
Lausanne and Geneva form a Swiss diocese immediately subject to Rome, whose see traces, on Marius Besson's recent research, to ancient Windisch. Bubulcus, first Bishop of Windisch, appears at the imperial Synod of Epao in 517, and Gramatius, the last, signed Clermont in 535 and Orleans in 541 and 549.

Between 549 and 585 the see split, its real seat moving to Avenches while the east joined Constance. St. Marius, consecrated at Avenches in May 574 and dead in 594, added years 455 to 581 to Prosper's Chronicle and may have moved the see to Lausanne, or it moved by 610. Lausanne served Lyons, then Besancon, until the French Concordat of 1801 detached it. Medieval bounds ran from the Aar near Soleure along the Jura to Lake Geneva.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-military-orde:
In twelfth-century Castile, the Military Order of Calatrava arose as the armed offshoot of the great Cistercian family. In the Cistercian Order, formed in 1098, many members had been knights or knights' sons, but at Calatrava the reverse happened: men who had been monks became knights. Monastic life itself was called a warfare, and it would be wrong to suppose those rough medieval warriors sought in the cloister only a comfortable refuge.

Both lives demanded heroic struggle, whether against one's passions or against the Moslems, and cloister austerities could hardly have seemed more dreadful than camp privations. Calatrava takes its name from a castle recovered from the Moslems in 1147 by Alfonso VII of Castile, on Castile's extreme southern border. It was a conquest harder to keep than to make when neither standing armies nor garrisons existed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oliva:
Oliva, a suppressed Cistercian abbey near Danzig, helped Christianize northeast Germany before fire, war, and suppression undid it. Founded with Pomeranian dukes' help between 1170 and 1178, it passed from Poland to the Teutonic Order, back to Poland, then to Prussia and Danzig.

Heathen Prussians burned it in 1224 and 1234, Hussites pillaged it in 1433, Danzig Protestants nearly destroyed it in 1577, and Swedes sacked it twice more. Suppressed in 1831, its three-naved brick church survives as Oliva's parish church, most other buildings being torn down. After Oliva passed to Poland in 1466, it stayed out of the Polish Cistercian province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-cord:
Pedro de Cordova was born at Cordova in Andalusia, Spain, about 1460 and dead on Santo Domingo island in 1525. He studied theology at Salamanca University and there joined the Dominicans. About 1510 he went to Santo Domingo, founding the order's Santa Cruz province. He defended the Indians zealously and befriended Las Casas.

His book, Christian Doctrine for the Indians' Instruction and Information by Way of History, was printed in 1544 at Mexico by Bishop Zumarraga's direction. Meant for the Indians' education, chiefly of the islands, it ranks among America's earliest known catechism books. Fray Pedro became the New World's first inquisitor. He enjoyed a model priest's reputation, highly respected by clergy, laity, and Indians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-gen:
Robert of Geneva became the antipope Clement VII, first antipope of the Great Schism. Born at Geneva in 1342, son of Count Amadeus III, he became prothonotary apostolic in 1359, Bishop of Therouanne in 1361, Archbishop of Cambrai in 1368, and cardinal in 1371. As legate in Upper Italy in 1376-78, seeking to crush rebellion in the Papal States, he reportedly ordered the massacre of 4,000 people at Cesena. That earned him the name executioner of Cesena.

French cardinals elected him at Fondi on 20 September 1378 against Urban VI. France, Scotland, Castile, Aragon, Navarre, Portugal, Savoy, Denmark, Norway, and some German states acknowledged him. Unable to hold Italy, he settled at Avignon, dependent on France. He chose cardinals, yet gave much of the Papal States to Louis II of Anjou and used simony and extortion to fund his court. He seems never to have sought an end to the schism. He died at Avignon in 1394.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-of-:
Thomas of Villanova, archbishop of Valencia, poured his revenues into the poor and earned the name father of the poor. Born at Fuentellana in 1488 to Alonso Tomas Garcia and Lucia Martinez, he grew up amid his parents' almsgiving. His father gave each Friday's mill earnings. His widowed mother clothed poor maidens.

At sixteen he entered Alcalá. He took degrees in arts and theology. He held the chair of arts, logic, and philosophy from 1514, teaching Encina and Soto. He declined Salamanca's chair of natural philosophy, joined the Augustinians in 1516, and was ordained in 1518. As archbishop from 1544 he reformed clergy, founded schools, and gave away nearly all his income. He died at Valencia on 8 September 1555.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-duke-of-a:
Spanish general Fernando Alvarez de Toledo, Duke of Alva, is the stern statesman portrayed here. Born in 1508 of a Castilian house boasting Byzantine imperial descent, he died at Thomar on 12 January 1582. Severe discipline from childhood trained him for war and statecraft. At sixteen he fought France, at seventeen Pavia's siege, in 1527 Turks in Hungary, winning Charles V's esteem across half a century of wars.

Chief fame rests on his 1567 mission to the riotous Netherlands, where Gueux opposition vexed Margaret of Parma's regency. Philip, born a Dutchman yet bent on Spanish absolutism, spurned mild counsels and demanded swift punishment for a rebellious, heretical land. Alva's Council of Troubles, executions, and taxes follow, with judgment that balances soldierly skill against pitiless rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ceva:
Thomas Ceva, a mathematician born at Milan in 1648, entered the Society of Jesus in 1663 and died in Milan in 1737. He wrote widely on mathematics and poetry, but his name survives for a single theorem in geometry. Ceva's theorem states that when three lines drawn from a triangle's corners to the opposite sides meet at one point, the product of the three distance ratios equals one.

He published the result in 1678, and geometers note it as the dual, or mirror counterpart, of the theorem of Menelaus. The entry is short, as befits a man remembered for one clean idea rather than a long career. It gives his dates, his order, and the theorem that keeps his name in textbooks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ungava:
Ungava was a Canadian territory lying north of the province of Quebec, cut off from the great Labrador peninsula in 1876. Its area of 354,961 square miles surpassed Quebec's own 351,873, and in 1912 the federal government annexed it to Quebec. It was bounded by Hudson Strait and Ungava Bay, by Labrador proper to the east, by Quebec to the south, and by Hudson and James Bays to the west.

Basques, Cabot in 1493, Weymouth in 1602, and Hudson in 1610 visited its coasts, while the Jesuits Dablon and Albanel crossed it by land toward Hudson Bay in 1661 and 1672. In the last century Oblate missionaries evangelized the Indians of the interior, and Moravian Brothers began work among the Eskimo in 1770. The entry sketches a vast northern land of coasts, bays, and tundra, known more to traders and missionaries than to settlers.
doe-osti-2586878-ornl-portable-diagnosti: ORNL's portable mirror diagnostics got their DOE package, and this report evaluates mirror performance. The pages detail the portable tools. The optics folks get their kit. The package was portable diagnostic. The performance was mirror. The folks were optics. The kit was optics.
doe-osti-2589167-heating-ventilation-air: HVAC for Revit got its OpenStudio analysis, and this DOE report optimizes the system design. The pages detail the ANA approach. The building engineers get their tool. The system was HVAC. The analysis was system. The engineers got tools. The design was system.
doe-osti-3016982-developing-source-term-: Source terms got database-developed, and this DOE text covers advanced reactors. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The database was source term. The data were nuclear. The reactors were advanced. The term was source.
doe-osti-3020505-s-amp-tr-jan-feb-2026-v: S&TR got Vera-Rubin-issued, and this DOE Jan/Feb 2026 text covers the observatory. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their data. The issue was observatory. The data were researcher. The 2026 was Jan/Feb. The Rubin was Vera.
doe-osti-3023633-developing-safe-effecti: Heavy metals got orally treated, and this DOE CRADA final develops safe poisoning cures. The pages detail the report findings. The medical folks get their closeout. The treatments were effective. The closeout was medical. The poisoning were metal. The available were orally.
doe-osti-3028187-applied-genomics-for-in: Algae getting DNA-tuned for industry got their DOE genomics lab, and this text breeds the microalgal strains. The pages detail the strain results. The bio folks get their data. The lab was applied. The DNA-tuned were algae. The strains were microalgal.
doe-osti-3399788-planetary-boundary-laye: PBLHT got remote-sensing-retrieved, and this DOE product covers boundary-layer heights. The pages detail the value findings. The climate folks get their data. The added was value. The data were climate. The PBLHT were retrievals. The heights were boundary-layer.
doe-osti-3874838-verification-plan-for-b: Particle accelerators promise researchers beam time — and broken promises stall science. Curt Lindenbaum's verification plan lays out how to check that beam hours and availability requirements are actually met. The plan keeps facilities honest about the uptime they owe their users.
dutt-mahabharata-adi-parva:
Dutt's prose Mahabharata opens with the Adi Parva, Englished in 1895. The Book of Beginnings traces the Bharata line from its first kings. The princes' youth and the famed dice game fill its later span.

Feuds take root as Pandava and Kaurava cousins grow up rivals. Teachers, marriages, and exile shape the heroes of the coming war. Dutt aimed to give English readers the whole vast epic in prose. His was the first full English Mahabharata of its kind ever made. The world's longest epic starts its immense arc in this opening book. Every later grief grows from seeds planted in these early chapters.
dutt-mahabharata-anushasana-parva:
Anushasana Parva, the Book of Instruction, comes in Dutt's 1905 English. Bhishma's teachings from the arrow-bed reach their end in this volume. The old warrior answers the king's last questions on right conduct.

Duty, charity, gifts, and the rites owed to gods and kin fill the talks. Precept stands on precept in the epic's great didactic manner. Bhishma blesses the king, then yields his life at the chosen hour. The book completes the moral frame of the whole Mahabharata. Dutt's plain prose keeps the old counsel clear for modern readers today. The farewell to Bhishma lands with quiet, earned force at the end.
dutt-mahabharata-shanti-parva:
Shanti Parva, the Book of Peace, appears in Dutt's 1903 English version. After the great war, the dying Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows. From that bed he teaches the young king through long, calm talks.

Law, kingship, duty, and the good life unfold in his final lessons. He speaks to a world shattered by war and kin-killing. His counsel mixes hard statecraft with deep thought on fate and release. Many call this book the epic's deep core of wisdom. Rulers and plain readers alike have mined its teachings for ages. Its calm tone after so much slaughter gives the lessons extra weight.
ex-voto-an-account-of-the-sacro-monte-or: Samuel Butler's 1890 account describes the Sacro Monte, or New Jerusalem, at Varallo-Sesia, a hillside shrine of chapels holding life-size tableaux of sacred scenes. He walks the reader through the chapels and their figures, judging the sculpture and painting as art as well as devotion. A closing section notices Tabachetti's remaining work at the sanctuary of Crea.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile-cy:
For decades, governments in Latin America's Southern Cone trusted Crypto AG machines to keep their most secret messages safe. The CIA's Minerva Secret reveals who really stood behind the Swiss company: the CIA itself, as a hidden owner.

Operation Condor states used the firm's devices without knowing their supplier was American intelligence, which could read what the machines appeared to protect. The briefing book tells how the secret was kept for so long and what it yielded to Washington. It is a story about trust in technology, and about how one hidden ownership deal quietly opened the secret cables of half a continent.
nasa-tm-19660020065-development-of-ablat:
Peter J LeBel and James M Russell III at Langley developed sensors that ride inside a heat shield. The sensors report how fast the shield wears away in flight. Their paper was given in Los Angeles in October 1965. An ablative shield protects a reentry vehicle by melting and flowing off. Knowing how fast the surface recedes during flight is the key measure. Three sensor kinds are named: make wire, light pipe, and spring wire types.

Flight data from inside a working shield are hard to get any other way. Ground tests cannot copy a real entry in full. Sensors that survive long enough to report give designers the truth about their shield. Advanced reentry vehicles, named in the title, were the direct users of this work.
nasa-tm-19670007218-an-integrating-spher:
James B. Heaney, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in December 1966. It presents a coating that lets integrating spheres work in the vacuum ultraviolet. An integrating sphere collects reflected light evenly so total reflectance can be measured, but standard smoked magnesium oxide coatings fail at short wavelengths.

Heaney's solution uses the fluorescent properties of sodium salicylate. The sphere is first coated with a durable magnesium oxide paint that reflects well where sodium salicylate glows. A thin salicylate layer goes on top, sensitive to the short-wave radiation bounced off the sample. The pairing also reflects the resulting fluorescent light reasonably well. The paper describes the instrument used and reports tests on several matte samples.
nasa-tm-19670014580-dim-light-photograph:
L. Dunkelman and a co-author, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, prepared this briefing in February 1966. It covers photographing faint space phenomena, and watching them by eye, from crewed spacecraft. The preface says the document copies the written information given to the Gemini VI and VII crews before their flights.

NASA Headquarters had asked for these experiments on an opportunity basis. The first section treats the twilight scene, a continuing study of Schirra's bands and aerosol layers. Long-exposure color photography could catch the higher, fainter layers of air. The last pages reproduce the checklists carried aboard both spacecraft.
nasa-tm-19700026393-an-analysis-of-the-r:
B. H. Batson prepared this internal note at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston on November 1, 1968. It analyzes the relative merits of various PCM code formats. PCM, or pulse code modulation, is a way to send data as coded pulses from a spacecraft, turning measured levels into ones and zeros.

Batson notes that the range instrumentation group allowed seven digital formats for such streams. All seven, he explains, are variants of three basic shapes for writing a bit. They are non-return-to-zero, split-phase, and return-to-zero forms. One key difference among them is the transmission bandwidth each one demands. The analysis weighs the formats against each other so engineers could pick with the trade-offs in view.
twenty-four-short-sermons-on-the-doctrin:
John Bovee Dods, pastor of the First Universalist Society at Taunton, Massachusetts, printed Twenty-Four Short Sermons on the Doctrine of Universal Salvation at Boston in 1832. Sermon one takes its text from Psalm 34: keep the tongue from evil, depart from evil, and seek peace.

Dods begins with self-preservation, the desire to lengthen life that clings to people even in pain and misery. Regulating the passions, he argues, does more for health and long life than climate or diet. Malice, envy, and revenge corrode body and soul alike, while tenderness, compassion, and hope multiply a person's years. Universalist preaching here starts from daily conduct rather than doctrine.
